title: Bangladesh to form wage board after garment protests shut factories
full_text:
DHAKA, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Bangladesh will set up a wage board on Sunday to review garment workers’ pay after protests shut dozens of factories and triggered clashes with police, putting fresh strain on the country’s key export industry.
Workers in the South Asian nation are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($245), more than double the current 12,500 taka, saying rising costs of food, housing, transport and healthcare have sharply eroded their purchasing power.
The dispute has raised concerns about disruption to an industry that employs about 4 million workers, generates more than 80% of Bangladesh’s export earnings and supplies clothing to many leading Western brands.
Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the government would formally constitute the wage board after discussions with labour leaders and industry representatives aimed at defusing the unrest.
Saturday’s protests prompted about 30 garment factories in Ashulia, a key manufacturing hub on the outskirts of Dhaka, to declare holidays, said Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of the Ashulia Industrial Police.
Hundreds of workers blocked a major intersection in the capital, while demonstrations in other industrial zones disrupted traffic and factory operations. Clashes between workers and police in Ashulia injured several people, including police officers, police said. Officers used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse protesters.
Chowdhury urged workers to return to work, saying the government’s decision to review the wage structure addressed their key demand.
He warned that prolonged factory closures and production disruptions could delay export shipments and payments from international buyers, creating further difficulties for manufacturers and workers.
Bangladesh’s ready-made garment industry, the world’s largest after China, contributes about 10% of gross domestic product and is the backbone of the economy.
Manufacturers, however, said the sector is facing mounting challenges, including rising production costs, periodic gas and electricity shortages, and uncertainty in energy markets linked to tensions in the Middle East.

Demand for hedging instruments, including put options and credit-default swaps, has accelerated following sharp declines in technology stocks and growing concerns about the financial risks associated with AI infrastructure spending.

CoreWeave, a major AI infrastructure provider, has attracted particularly strong demand for downside protection.
Trading volumes for put options tied to the company reached record levels in October, according to Cboe Global Markets data.
Popular contracts include options expiring in 2028 that would benefit from CoreWeave shares falling to $35, compared with approximately $55 recently.
Concerns have also spread to corporate debt markets.
The cost of insuring against defaults by Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle recently climbed to its highest level since 2021, according to bond data provider Solve.

Trading firms are developing new financial products to address risks associated with AI computing infrastructure.
Jump Trading has launched a computing-power trading desk offering derivatives designed to protect data center operators against falling chip rental prices.
Rental rates for Nvidia B300 chips have increased approximately 56% this year to $7.56 per hour, according to Silicon Data.

title: Trump calls $50 million contract for ex-lawyer Habba Mildon ’not acceptable’
full_text:
By Gram Slattery and Jasper Ward
PALM BEACH, Oct 31 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Saturday it was "unacceptable" for one of his former lawyers, Alina Habba Mildon, to secure a $50 million contract for herself while working at the US Department of Justice.
"I thought it was totally obnoxious and outrageous, and it’s not acceptable," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. "Not acceptable at all."
The New York Times reported last week that the family of Julio Herrera Velutini, a Venezuelan banker facing US felony bribery charges before striking a plea deal in August 2025, guaranteed Habba Mildon more than $50 million over four years. The deal, according to the newspaper, would pay $10 million a year plus bonuses.
Trump said he told Habba Mildon he did not want her to be paid and called the episode "terrible."
Habba Mildon was serving as the acting US attorney in New Jersey when she signed the contract with Herrera’s family company, Concord Partners, days after it was registered in late October 2025, the New York Times reported.
By the time she started her employment with the Herrera family, a court had disqualified her from serving as US attorney. She resigned on December 8 and was appointed a senior adviser to the attorney general the same day, and was still in that role when, according to the New York Times, she started at Concord on January 1.
Trump pardoned Herrera on January 15, 2026, according to the Justice Department’s website.
Habba Mildon last week said she was never paid for a pardon, never met with anyone at the White House or Justice Department about a pardon, and never did any work for a pardon for anyone.
The Justice Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Investing.com -- Apple Inc (NASDAQ:AAPL) reclaimed its position as the world’s most valuable publicly traded company on Friday, edging past NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) as mounting skepticism surrounding aggressive artificial intelligence spending prompted a rotation into more capital-disciplined balance sheets. Even with a 1.2% dip on the day, the iPhone maker closed with a market capitalization of $5.03 trillion, while a 4.2% slide in Nvidia lowered the chipmaker’s valuation to $4.93 trillion.
The milestone marks the first time Apple has surpassed Nvidia since a brief stint in late July. Against that backdrop, Apple’s measured stance on infrastructure investment has transformed the stock into a preferred haven within the Magnificent Seven cohort. Shares are up 27% year-to-date, more than double Nvidia’s second-place advance, bolstered by a 3% gain over the past month that diverged sharply from peers.
The divergence highlights mounting institutional focus on balance sheet health, particularly as soaring capital commitments begin to erode fundamental cash generation among hyper-scalers. Alphabet disclosed negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion for the third quarter, while Amazon reported a trailing twelve-month negative free cash flow deficit of $42.4 billion as infrastructure deployment accelerated.
With borrowing costs elevated, peers have increasingly turned to debt markets to bridge those cash deficits rather than relying strictly on organic operational funding. Apple, by contrast, is expected to generate expanding free cash flow, offering investors immediate liquidity resilience while the broader sector navigates a protracted wait for enterprise AI monetization.

title: Iran offers 48-hour Hormuz reopening plan as Trump signals progress in talks
full_text:
Investing.com -- Iran has proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington meets its conditions, offering a breakthrough in talks to end the war as both sides warn that renewed fighting could spread regionally.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Qatari mediators had helped shorten Tehran’s seven-day reopening proposal. Under the revised sequence, the U.S. would take steps on the first day, and shipping would resume on the second.
President Donald Trump said negotiations were “going fine” and Iran wanted a deal, although he added that Washington was not in a hurry. He also renewed threats against Iranian nuclear facilities, including the site known as Pickaxe Mountain.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump had not decided whether to launch fresh strikes and that a diplomatic settlement remained possible. An Iranian delegation was in Doha for consultations with mediators, with no direct U.S.-Iran talks planned.
Tehran’s demands include sanctions relief, the release of frozen funds, restored oil waivers, and recognition of a shipping route designated with Oman. Iran also wants a reduced U.S. military presence and an end to attacks on Lebanon.
Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei said a letter from Vice President JD Vance signaled a more conciliatory U.S. tone, but insisted Tehran would not reopen Hormuz before its conditions were met.
The diplomatic opening came alongside escalating military warnings. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered commanders to prepare an immediate response to any attack without geographical restrictions, and Iranian officials threatened strikes against a wider range of targets.
Shipping risks remain acute. Iran’s navy said a tanker caught fire after striking mines east of Hormuz, without identifying the vessel or reporting the crew’s condition. U.S. Central Command said its blockade of Iranian ports had redirected 144 commercial ships.
Disruption to the waterway continues to threaten global energy supplies. Germany’s gas storage industry warned that reserves stood at 61.35% ahead of winter, below the country’s 80% target, partly reflecting war-driven energy costs.
The coming days could test whether the proposed shipping arrangement can advance before Washington and Tehran resolve their disputes.

title: Binance to resume crypto withdrawals in phases after record $6 billion hack
full_text:
Investing.com -- Binance said it would begin restoring customer withdrawals in stages on Sunday after a record cryptocurrency theft exceeding $6 billion forced the world’s largest digital asset exchange to suspend transactions and raised concerns about security across the industry.
The exchange said the first phase would run from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m. Singapore time on November 1, with additional cryptocurrencies and blockchain networks restored after security and stability checks.
Binance said it would prioritize assets based on customer withdrawal demand over the previous week, allowing services to resume gradually rather than reopening all transactions simultaneously.
The announcement follows a breach disclosed Thursday that prompted Binance to halt withdrawals early Friday in Asia.
The FBI attributed the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group, which was previously linked to the $1.5 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance said it had replaced approximately 90% of the stolen cryptocurrencies and reiterated that customers would not bear the financial losses.
The stolen assets included Bitcoin, Ether and dollar-backed stablecoins USDT and USDC.
Co-CEO Richard Teng said the exchange could cover the losses through cryptocurrency holdings accumulated from its operating revenue.
Fellow co-CEO Yi He indicated that Binance’s annual revenue would be sufficient to absorb the financial impact.
Bitcoin traded near $77,700 on Sunday, approximately 5% below its Thursday high before the attack, as major cryptocurrencies showed relatively limited price movements.
The exchange holds approximately $135 billion in assets, significantly exceeding the roughly $29 billion held by rival OKX, according to DefiLlama.
Binance also maintains its Secure Asset Fund for Users, established in 2018 to protect customers during exceptional incidents. The emergency reserve has typically been maintained near $1 billion.
Investigators are examining a potentially compromised software engineer’s laptop and other possible entry points, although Binance said it had found no evidence that private wallet keys were exposed.
The incident has intensified scrutiny of cryptocurrency security amid concerns that hackers are increasingly using artificial intelligence for reconnaissance and social engineering.

title: Hanwha secures $269 million U.S. Navy shipbuilding contract, eyes more orders
full_text:
Investing.com -- South Korea’s Hanwha Defense USA has secured a $269 million contract to build a medium landing ship for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, marking its first U.S. naval shipbuilding order since acquiring Philadelphia’s Philly Shipyard in 2024.
The agreement with U.S. maritime services company TOTE Services covers construction of one Medium Landing Ship (LSM), with options for three additional vessels.
The 2,687-ton, 100-meter ship is designed to support military operations in contested waters, including the Indo-Pacific region.
Construction at Hanwha Philly Shipyard is scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027, with the program’s first vessel expected to be delivered in 2030.
Hanwha was selected through a competitive bidding process launched in July under TOTE Services’ vessel construction management program.
The company secured the contract based on competitive pricing and its acceptance of the program’s subcontract terms.
TOTE Services received a $2.2 billion contract earlier this year to oversee construction of up to eight vessels, supporting the Navy and Marine Corps’ planned 35-ship LSM fleet.
The program aims to expand U.S. naval shipbuilding capacity and accelerate deliveries through coordinated construction across multiple domestic shipyards.
Hanwha acquired Philly Shipyard in December 2024 and has since invested in workforce development and production technology to prepare the facility for military contracts.
The shipyard has previously delivered four National Security Multi-Mission Vessels under TOTE Services’ construction management model.
Hanwha Defense USA is also pursuing a controlling stake in the Philadelphia facility as part of its expansion into American defense manufacturing.
TOTE Services is continuing discussions with Bollinger Shipyards and Fincantieri Marinette Marine about their participation in the landing ship program.
The contract represents another step in Hanwha’s efforts to establish a stronger position in the U.S. defense shipbuilding market.

The FBI, working alongside the U.S. Secret Service and the Internal Revenue Service’s criminal investigation division, has been tracking movements of the stolen digital assets.

The exchange expects to restore customer withdrawals by Sunday as it works to complete recovery efforts.
Binance reiterated that it would absorb the entire financial impact of the breach, promising that customers would not suffer losses from the incident.
The unprecedented theft has raised fresh concerns about security across the cryptocurrency industry as digital asset platforms seek broader institutional and retail adoption.
TraderTraitor has previously been linked to several high-profile cryptocurrency attacks, including the $1.5 billion theft from Bybit in 2025.
North Korean hackers have also been accused of carrying out a separate cryptocurrency theft worth approximately $620 million in 2022.
The FBI’s attribution comes amid renewed discussion of potential diplomatic engagement between Washington and Pyongyang.
Trump has recently suggested another meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un could take place this year, although he later expressed uncertainty about whether either side was seeking talks.

title: What’s next for Euro bonds and the euro after Lagarde’s resignation?
full_text:
Investing.com -- European bond yields are expected to decline next year, and the euro could recover against the U.S. dollar, as ECB President Christine Lagarde’s early departure is unlikely to alter the central bank’s monetary policy outlook, according to UBS.
Lagarde announced her resignation effective February 7, 2027, hours before the European Central Bank held interest rates unchanged amid persistent inflation pressures and rising energy costs.
UBS expects a smooth leadership transition, arguing that inflation, wages, economic growth and financing conditions will remain the primary drivers of interest rates.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year, with inflation running at roughly double its 2% target.
Although policymakers have signaled further tightening may be necessary, UBS believes the central bank will wait for clearer evidence of persistent inflation before acting.
A December rate increase remains possible, particularly if higher energy prices trigger broader inflationary pressures.
Still, UBS expects Eurozone sovereign borrowing costs to decline into 2027, despite continued volatility in French government bonds.
France’s fiscal and political challenges could push sovereign spreads wider without credible budget consolidation.
UBS said the ECB could respond to disruptive market pressures through flexible reinvestment of maturing bonds, with its unused Transmission Protection Instrument providing another option.
The bank believes markets are pricing in excessive tightening, with expectations for another 75 basis points of ECB increases appearing difficult to justify.
It favors selectively extending duration in high-quality European bonds, particularly short- and medium-term maturities, including agency, covered and investment-grade corporate debt.
Longer maturities remain less attractive amid fiscal concerns and substantial bond issuance.
For currencies, UBS maintained its bullish euro outlook, forecasting EUR/USD to recover toward 1.16 by year-end.
The bank believes the euro’s recent decline has exceeded what underlying economic fundamentals would suggest.
Still, energy prices, monetary policy differences, sovereign spreads and geopolitical developments could keep currency markets volatile.
UBS also recommends progressively reducing excess U.S. dollar exposure where appropriate.

title: Saudi Arabia’s economy contracts 3.8% as war disrupts oil production
full_text:
Investing.com -- Saudi Arabia’s economy contracted for a second consecutive quarter as the war involving Iran and escalating conflict with Yemen’s Houthi rebels disrupted oil production and exports, threatening one of the kingdom’s weakest economic performances in years.
Gross domestic product declined 3.8% year over year in the third quarter, according to preliminary figures released Sunday by Saudi Arabia’s General Authority for Statistics.
The contraction was smaller than the 4.7% decline recorded in the second quarter but marked the first consecutive quarterly declines since 2023.
Oil sector activity plunged 20.4%, improving from a 24.8% contraction in the previous quarter, as attacks on energy infrastructure continued to disrupt production and shipments.
Non-oil activity expanded 1.9%, highlighting the relative resilience of industries central to Saudi Arabia’s economic diversification strategy.
The figures reflect disruptions from the eight-month U.S.-Iran conflict, which has triggered attacks on Gulf energy facilities and restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has partially offset the disruption by redirecting crude shipments through a pipeline connecting its eastern oil fields to a Red Sea export terminal.
The third-quarter data also captures a temporary shutdown of that pipeline in September following attacks, but predates the subsequent recovery in Saudi crude exports to wartime highs.
The economic outlook has become more uncertain following an escalation in fighting between Saudi-led forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in October.
Houthi missile and drone attacks disrupted flights at Riyadh’s airport, forced changes to major investment events and interrupted activity in the capital’s financial district.
Although Brent crude has traded above $115 a barrel, concerns are increasingly shifting toward the impact of the conflict on non-oil businesses.
The International Monetary Fund said Saudi Arabia’s financial reserves and alternative oil-export infrastructure were helping cushion the economic damage, leaving the kingdom better positioned than several Gulf neighbors.
Saudi authorities previously projected a 3.6% economic contraction in 2026 and raised their expected budget deficit to 4.9% of GDP.

title: South Korea exports surge 93.7% in October, fastest growth since 1974
full_text:
Investing.com -- South Korea’s exports surged 93.7% in October from a year earlier, marking their strongest growth in more than five decades as booming semiconductor shipments and artificial intelligence demand powered overseas sales, government data showed Sunday.
Exports from Asia’s fourth-largest economy reached $115.28 billion, exceeding economists’ median forecast for a 93.2% increase.
The expansion accelerated from September’s 83.7% annual gain and represented the fastest export growth since January 1974, according to the trade ministry.
South Korea’s export performance is closely watched as an indicator of global trade conditions, particularly demand for electronics, semiconductors and other manufactured goods.
Semiconductor exports jumped 259.4% from a year earlier, supported by elevated chip prices and strong shipment volumes.
The trade ministry attributed the increase to sustained investment in computing infrastructure by major global technology companies competing for leadership in artificial intelligence.
Computer exports recorded an even sharper increase, soaring 496.6% as demand for servers supporting AI services continued to expand.
The figures highlight the growing contribution of AI-related technology spending to South Korea’s export performance, with semiconductor manufacturers benefiting from expanding data center investments.
The ministry also cited favorable calendar effects, as differences in the timing of the Chuseok holiday resulted in more working days during October than a year earlier.
That comparison helped amplify the annual growth rate, alongside strong underlying demand for technology products.
Imports also increased sharply, rising 36% year over year to $72.78 billion, compared with a 26% increase in September.
The import growth was the strongest since January 2022, reflecting a substantial acceleration in the value of goods entering the country.
South Korea recorded a trade surplus of $42.50 billion in October, down from the record $49.97 billion surplus registered in September.
The narrowing surplus came as import growth accelerated, although export revenues remained substantially higher than the country’s monthly import bill.

title: Who are the spillover winners from the AI export boom in Asia?
full_text:
Investing.com -- Taiwan is emerging as the biggest domestic beneficiary of Asia’s artificial intelligence export boom, followed by South Korea, as stronger technology demand boosts economic activity, government revenues and investment, according to Bank of America.
The bank said AI-related exports have become a major growth driver for Taiwan, South Korea and China, although the economic benefits are spreading unevenly across the three markets.
Year-to-date exports have increased 57% year over year in South Korea, 44% in Taiwan and 21% in China, according to BofA’s analysis.
Despite South Korea recording the strongest export growth, Taiwan is expected to experience the largest domestic spillover effects.
BofA attributed the differences to the relative size of each economy’s technology sector, production capacity constraints and broader economic conditions.
Taiwan’s substantial exposure to technology manufacturing means stronger external demand can translate into wider domestic economic gains.
South Korea also stands to benefit significantly, with the export expansion supporting domestic activity and government finances.
China is benefiting from stronger technology exports, but weaker domestic demand and economic headwinds are limiting the broader impact.
The differences are also shaping fiscal policy across the region.
BofA said rising exports have increased government tax revenues in all three economies, creating opportunities for additional public spending.
In Taiwan and South Korea, higher fiscal receipts are helping finance transfers and investment, providing another channel through which export growth supports domestic demand.
China has not experienced a comparable spending boost, partly reflecting financial constraints facing local governments.
The uneven economic effects are expected to produce different monetary policy responses.

At least 60 vessels equipped with makeshift anti-drone defenses have been documented passing through Istanbul’s Bosporus Strait since August, according to photographs reviewed by the newspaper.
The images, captured by maritime analyst Yoruk Isik, show tankers carrying protective structures around vulnerable areas, including engines, steering equipment, and bridge windows.
Nearly all the vessels identified are subject to U.S. or other Western sanctions for transporting Russian oil.
The defensive measures resemble equipment used on military vehicles and infrastructure in Ukraine, where drones have become a central weapon in the conflict.
Analysts said the nets and cages are intended to intercept incoming drones before they strike critical ship components.
Some vessels have also attached rubber tires along their sides to protect engines and rudders from attacks that could leave tankers disabled.
The modifications reflect growing concerns over Ukraine’s campaign against Russia’s shadow fleet, which transports oil outside conventional Western shipping and insurance arrangements.
Ukraine has intensified attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, including refineries and oil tankers, seeking to reduce export revenues that help finance Moscow’s war effort.
The commander of Ukraine’s drone forces claimed in September that Ukrainian operations had disabled 300 Russian shadow-fleet vessels since July. That figure has not been independently verified.
Security analysts said the campaign could also place pressure on Russia’s financial system.
Many aging shadow-fleet tankers rely on insurance and financial backing from Russian state-supported banks, potentially exposing those institutions to losses from damaged vessels.
Ukraine escalated attacks on the fleet in 2025 as Washington pushed Kyiv and Moscow toward negotiations to end the war.
Russian oil shipments remain a major source of foreign currency for Moscow, making the tankers an economically significant target.

Investing.com -- Macau’s casino gaming revenue fell for a fifth consecutive month in October, as weaker spending by wealthy gamblers outweighed increased tourist arrivals during China’s Golden Week holiday.
Gross gaming revenue declined 10% from a year earlier to 21.68 billion patacas ($2.68 billion), according to figures released Sunday by Macau’s Gaming Inspection and Coordination Bureau.

The downturn continued despite a strong recovery in tourist arrivals during the Golden Week holiday, traditionally one of the busiest periods for Macau’s casinos.
The gambling hub welcomed approximately 1.14 million visitors during the holiday, representing a 15.5% increase from the previous year.
Yet the additional visitors failed to generate a corresponding increase in gambling expenditure, according to analysts at Jefferies.
The figures suggest that stronger tourism demand has not been sufficient to offset reduced spending among higher-value casino customers.
Macau also recorded 3.2 million visitor arrivals in September, an increase of 16% year over year, indicating that tourism growth remained relatively resilient.
Complete visitor arrival figures for October are expected to be released later in November.
A cooling Chinese stock market has added to pressure on casino spending, reversing some of the wealth effects that supported gambling demand last year.
Macau’s gaming industry benefited from an artificial intelligence-driven equity market rally during the second half of 2025, which helped lift spending among affluent visitors.
That earlier recovery has also created tougher year-over-year comparisons for casino operators in 2026.
The prolonged slowdown affects major operators including Sands China, Galaxy Entertainment, Wynn Macau, MGM China and Melco International, which depend heavily on visitors from mainland China.

title: Trump White House maps path to govern without Congress if Democrats win
full_text:
By Nandita Bose and Tim Reid
WASHINGTON, Nov 1 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans.
Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the White House Counsel’s Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at "what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court," the White House official said.
The planning underscores a paradox of Tuesday’s midterm elections: Capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and constrain his spending priorities. But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term.
Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favor Democrats to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call.
For the past month, Trump has held rallies across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027.
The White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative.
"This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.
Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said.
Federal agencies have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the people with knowledge of the plans said.
Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can move forward using money already appropriated by Congress, two of the people said.
He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees more say in which government programs receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval.
Trump has been briefed on the preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said.
When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the people said, "very comfortable."
GOVERNING WITHOUT CONGRESS
Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress’ approval or new laws.
A major exception was Trump’s massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025.
"President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power," said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides nonpartisan political analysis. "I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities."
Trump has repeatedly invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation. Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him.
A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles.
Control of the Senate would allow Democrats to block Trump’s judicial and executive-branch nominees, including any Supreme Court pick.
"I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to approve any of the president’s appointments," said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections.
Democrats could also refuse to pass Trump-backed legislation. But Trump could veto Democratic legislation he doesn’t like, and Democrats are unlikely to have enough votes in the House to override him.
Courts could block executive actions that exceed Trump’s legal authority. The White House plans to seek legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine what Trump can do without Congress and how to defend those actions if they are challenged in court, one of the people said.
DEMOCRATIC INVESTIGATIONS
One challenge, however, cannot be sidestepped through executive action: congressional investigations.
Reuters previously reported that senior House Democrats and committee aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to examine whether Trump has used his presidential power to benefit himself, allies or donors.
Trump aides have been preparing for that prospect for months, all three people said.
White House lawyers have been briefing political appointees and agency leaders on how to handle congressional inquiries, document requests and subpoenas, one person said. They have advised officials to be careful about what they put in writing.
They also sought a Justice Department opinion that could allow Trump to invoke executive privilege to shield communications with private advisers from congressional scrutiny, the person said.

Binance said it had now covered 95% of the stolen assets. It said after an initial spike, withdrawals were stabilizing.
The heist, which analysts believe may be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts, and the pace of withdrawals is an early test of whether customers trust the exchange with their money after the attack. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs.
A Binance spokesperson said in an emailed statement: “Withdrawal volumes spiked at the beginning, however we are seeing a sharp downward trend and withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity."
The spokesperson said the withdrawals represented a very small percentage of assets under management.
"Deposits are also significant. We will keep you updated. Rest assured that market conditions are stable,” the spokesperson said.
The world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange recorded more than $3.5 billion in net outflows on Sunday, crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboard. Binance did not comment on the DefiLlama data.
Binance, which was founded in China, said the rollout for withdrawals would be carried out in phases, prioritising user demand. The first phase covered 15 tokens including bitcoin, ether and those involving some USDC and USDT stablecoins and dogecoin.
"We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand," Binance said in an earlier article posted on X.
Binance said earlier on Sunday that it had covered $6 billion of stolen cryptocurrencies by using company money to buy replacement tokens. The remaining 5% of stolen tokens consist of assets that are less liquid and may take longer to source in the required amounts, according to the exchange.
FBI TIES ATTACK TO NORTH KOREAN UNIT
The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack.
Pyongyang has for years denied using state-linked cyber units for espionage, financial theft and revenue generation. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not respond to requests for comment.
Law enforcement observed members of the unit converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology.
Analysts had also blamed North Korea for the heist.
The bulk of the theft unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
US President Donald Trump, however, said on Saturday it remained unclear whether North Korea was involved.
"We don’t know if it’s North Korea — but if it is, we’ll talk to North Korea about it," Trump told reporters on Saturday in comments posted by a White House account on X.
BINANCE VOWS TO BEAR FINANCIAL COSTS
Binance has been working with industry partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located as of Friday, it said.
The exchange has repeatedly said it would bear the financial impact of the funds stolen in the hack. It has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses.
The money spent buying replacement tokens came from Binance’s $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund and its corporate treasury, it said on X.
Co-CEO Yi He said on Saturday that Binance would use 50% of its SAFU funds, while the company committed to replenishing the fund to about $1 billion.
Richard Teng, the other co-CEO, has said that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.
Crypto prices fell on Friday, while Binance sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe after the hack.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
BINANCE FOUNDER THANKS US LAW ENFORCEMENT
In a post on X that quoted the FBI statement on North Korea’s involvement, Binance founder Changpeng Zhao thanked the agency for its support. Binance did not respond to a request for comment on North Korea’s involvement.
Zhao, who was convicted in the US of failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program before being pardoned by Trump last year, said US law enforcement agencies provided vital help, including by tracking and freezing the stolen assets.
"A tweet can’t fully express our gratitude. Many crypto bros may not realize, a lot of the ’why bitcoin didn’t drop more?’ credit goes to them," Zhao wrote, referring to US law enforcement agencies.

title: Serbians mark railway disaster that led to rise of victorious student movement
full_text:
By Fedja Grulovic
NOVI SAD, Serbia, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Tens of thousands of people gathered at a Serbian railway station on Sunday to mark the anniversary of a deadly roof collapse that gave rise to the protest movement that toppled longtime President Aleksandar Vucic in an election a week ago.
Crowds converged from across the city of Novi Sad on the main train station, where the concrete awning crashed down shortly before noon on November 1, 2024, killing 16 people.
Mourners observed 16 minutes of silence before laying wreaths, flowers and candles near the site.
"On a personal, emotional, and social level, I hope for a collective healing," said Zorana Sijan Oborina, a student supporter.
The disaster, which struck at a station renovated under a China-backed high-speed rail project, ignited Serbia’s massive nationwide anti-corruption protest movement, culminating in last week’s election victory by a student-led bloc.
Protesters saw the collapse as symptomatic of corruption under Vucic. The protests forced resignations, including that of the construction minister, a government reshuffle and eventually snap elections.
Prosecutors indicted 13 people over the collapse, but pretrial proceedings have stalled. The defendants denied any wrongdoing.
"I hope we have finally realised that we shouldn’t wait ... years to change what is bad, especially when it costs human lives," said Jelena Trajkovic, 32, an academic from Novi Sad.
On October 25, the Student List, a group that includes academics, professionals, farmers, actors and activists chosen by student assemblies, secured 141 seats in the 250-member parliament, according to a preliminary tally. Final results are due in coming days and not expected to change the outcome.
Vucic, standing as the candidate for prime minister from his SNS party at the end of his presidential term, acknowledged defeat and left office. A presidential election is expected before the end of the year.

full_text:
By Lewis Krauskopf
NEW YORK, Oct 30 (Reuters) - US midterm elections, a heavy slate of corporate earnings and the monthly jobs report will further test stock investors next week, after a series of setbacks for the market-leading AI trade.
The latest AI turbulence stemmed from disappointing quarterly results of Alphabet and Amazon , two hyperscalers spending massively on data centers, while shares of semiconductor company Intel tumbled nearly 29% on Friday following its report.
Dragged down by tech and AI-related stocks, the S&P 500 sank 1.8% on Friday while the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.9%.
The quarterly results intensified concerns about financing and financial returns needed to support the AI investment theme at the heart of the US bull stock market. The questions are likely to persist, with Apple, AMD and Palantir among the major tech and AI players due to report next week. Also, the midterm elections could determine the outlook for AI regulation.
The stock market "seems a bit troubled to me, and I think that really stems from the AI fears that seem to be persistent, if not building," said Marta Norton, chief investment strategist at retirement and wealth services provider Empower. "There is still some digestion around what we saw with earnings this week."
MIDTERM VOTE COULD AFFECT AI
Tuesday’s elections will determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress away from President Donald Trump’s Republican party. Democrats are widely predicted to win the House of Representatives, but the Senate is more in doubt. Republicans controlled both chambers of Congress during the first two years of the Trump administration.
Investors are bracing for increasing pushback on data centers, whose impact on energy costs and the environment has led to intense public opposition. Despite doubts that any viable legislation will pose serious risks to AI investment, regardless of which party wins, a Democratic sweep is expected to bring more scrutiny. Investors are also watching local and state races in Texas and elsewhere on Tuesday for their implications for the data-center buildout.
"To the extent that the Democrats really do have a significant blue wave, I think that will be seen as negative for both the AI names, for tech to some extent in general, and maybe even for the market as a whole," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments.
Defense and healthcare are other stock market areas that could be sensitive to the election results. Any shift in Washington could affect the outlook for fiscal spending that could reverberate through asset prices. A Democratic sweep could bring more regulatory scrutiny, including for Wall Street banks and crypto firms.
ALSO ON TAP: APPLE, AMD RESULTS, JOBS DATA
Robust earnings performance has underpinned equity gains so far in 2026. With over half of the S&P 500 having reported third-quarter results, overall earnings were on pace to rise 31.6% for the period, according to LSEG IBES data on Friday.
Investors were punishing some reports. For example, Caterpillar shares sank 9% on Thursday after the company stuck to its annual sales growth forecast despite strong demand for its power equipment from data centers.
"The earnings bar is very high," said Chris Galipeau, head market strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute. "And if you miss or don’t jump over that bar, you’re in trouble."
Apple reports on Monday, with the iPhone maker’s shares up about 27% so far this year. Results are also expected from semiconductor companies AMD and Qualcomm as well as Palantir, which offers another view of the AI trade. McDonald’s, Amgen and ConocoPhillips are among over 100 S&P 500 companies that are due to report next week.
Next Friday’s employment report for October will give a critical read into the health of the US economy.
Data on Thursday showed the US economy in the third quarter grew at its fastest pace in a year, as consumers maintained robust spending and businesses doubled down on investment in AI. The Federal Reserve this week upgraded its assessment of the economy as it held interest rates steady.
"I think the missing piece of this strong economic growth narrative is the lack of job growth," said Matthew Miskin, co-chief investment strategist at Manulife John Hancock Investments.
Other areas of the market have picked up the slack as AI and related technology stocks have struggled. For October, the energy and financial sectors posted solid monthly gains, as did defensive groups such as utilities and healthcare. The S&P 500 was last up over 10% on the year.
"The market is much more broad than people generally want to give it credit for," Galipeau said.

title: Russian strikes cut power to thousands in Ukraine as drones damage Russian facility
full_text:
By Max Hunder and Alessandra Prentice
Nov 1 (Reuters) - Russian strikes left hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian households without power on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, while Russian authorities reported major damage to an industrial site following Ukrainian drone attacks on Nizhny Novgorod region.
Even as a six-day local ceasefire held on its final day around the Russian-controlled Ukrainian town of Oleshky, there was no letup in fighting elsewhere along the front line and both sides kept up long-range air attacks.
Zelenskiy said Russia had hit power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households.
"The intensity of the strikes is very high, and the Russians are seeking to maximally exploit the deficit of ballistic missile interceptors," he said on Telegram.
He said Ukraine, meanwhile, had hit the Kamensky plant in Russia’s Rostov region, which he said was involved in the manufacture of Russian missiles.
The governor of Ternopil region in western Ukraine, Taras Pastukh, said a Russian attack on infrastructure in a town in the region had knocked out power to localities. Emergency crews were working to restore it.
Moscow did not comment on the reported Ukrainian attack in Rostov. In Nizhny Novgorod region, however, Governor Gleb Nikitin said a large-scale overnight Ukrainian drone attack caused "significant damage" to an industrial facility.
He did not identify the site that was hit. The region is home to the NORSI oil refinery, one of Russia’s largest.
Overall, Russia’s Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 235 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight.
Ukraine’s air force said it had shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones launched by Russia since Saturday evening. In its morning update, the air force said dozens of Russian drones were still in the air as of Sunday morning. Six separate drone alerts had been issued in Kyiv since midnight.
FUEL SUPPLIES
Nizhny Novgorod’s regional government did not identify the facility that was struck, but it said it was taking steps to ensure gas stations were supplied with fuel, urging motorists to "buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying," Interfax reported.
The warning suggests the damaged facility may have been linked to the region’s oil-refining or fuel-supply infrastructure. Kyiv did not immediately claim responsibility for the Nizhny Novgorod attack.
On Friday, Russia said Ukraine had resumed strikes on its oil refineries and accused Kyiv of ignoring a request from US President Donald Trump to stop such attacks, which Trump has blamed for raising the cost of diesel before US midterm elections next week.
Ukraine says it supports a full ceasefire on energy targets, including its own battered power grid, but that Moscow is unwilling to agree to this.
In an interview with state TV channel Vesti on Sunday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the energy sector, did not mention the Nizhny Novgorod strike, but said Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries were adding to global fuel market imbalances and affecting prices.

title: US judge dismisses Trump election lawsuit in Alaska
full_text:
By Jan Wolfe and Mike Scarcella
Nov 1 (Reuters) - A federal judge on Sunday threw out a lawsuit by President Donald Trump’s administration seeking to block Alaska from certifying a loss by Republican Senator Dan Sullivan in Tuesday’s midterm elections if votes for a rival who shares his name could have changed the outcome.
The ruling by US District Judge Sharon Gleason in Anchorage was the latest blow to Trump’s efforts to assert a greater federal role in elections, which under the US Constitution are administered by the states.
Democratic former US Representative Mary Peltola is challenging Sullivan in the race, whose outcome could prove critical for determining whether Trump’s fellow Republicans can retain control of the Senate in the midterms. Democrats need a net gain of at least four seats in November’s midterm elections to gain control of the Senate.
Alaska’s ballot features the names of the incumbent senator, Daniel S. Sullivan, and Peltola, as well as a retired teacher whose name is Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., and another long-shot candidate.
Peltola has denied involvement in any effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan, who lives in a remote fishing village, to enter the race, saying at a rally that she is "not interested in tricking voters." The retired teacher has denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion, but has said he would prefer Peltola winning over the incumbent senator.
In her decision, Gleason wrote that the administration’s proposal to segregate ballots would violate the right of voters in Alaska to a secret ballot, and dismissed the case on the basis that the federal government lacked the necessary legal standing to bring it.
"The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ’investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote, referring to the Trump administration’s lawsuit.
The Justice Department said in a court filing it intends to appeal the ruling. In a statement, it said the judge’s order dismissing the lawsuit was on procedural grounds. Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled "in an attempt to rig outcomes," the Justice Department said.
Alaska officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the ruling.
The American Civil Liberties Union, which intervened in the lawsuit in support of Alaska, said the judge rebuffed a Justice Department effort to "throw out Alaska’s election results before a single ballot was counted."
"This administration keeps trying to tilt the midterms, and today (Sunday) it lost again," the ACLU said.
ELECTION OVERSIGHT
The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote. Critics, including Democratic and some Republican election officials, view the moves as federal overreach.
The lawsuit filed by the Justice Department on October 22 challenged the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan. According to the lawsuit, he is running "with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan into voting for him." The administration said that certifying the election could violate the federal government’s duty to protect the integrity of elections.
The suit sought to temporarily bar Alaska election officials from certifying a Peltola victory in the event that assigning all of Daniel J. Sullivan’s votes to the incumbent would have changed the results. The lawsuit said that, in such a scenario, Gleason should investigate whether voters who selected Daniel J. Sullivan had instead intended to support the incumbent.
’BALLOT STACKING’
The New York Times reported on October 28 that Peltola campaign staff members had worked with a Democratic operative from Ohio to find another Dan Sullivan to run to peel votes from the Republican senator. Reuters has not verified the report.
It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken. Both parties have engaged in "ballot stacking" by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents.
Trump, who has told reporters he ordered the Justice Department to file the lawsuit, has called for Peltola to be criminally prosecuted. The Justice Department has brought criminal charges against a number of Trump’s adversaries.
Peltola’s campaign had called the lawsuit meritless.

TOKYO, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Japan’s manufacturing sector expanded at its slowest pace in seven months in October as output and new orders lost momentum while cost pressures picked up, a business survey showed on Monday.

• Overseas demand remained supportive, but export order growth was the weakest since March. Survey respondents cited stronger demand from Asian markets, including China, North America, Africa and the Middle East.
• Employment growth held steady and stayed close to the fastest seen in the past eight-and-a-half years. The backlog of work accelerated, with some firms also reporting input delivery delays.
• Input price inflation accelerated in October, while output charge inflation eased to a six-month low. Stocks of purchases increased at the fastest rate in almost four years as firms sought to guard against further price rises.

title: Bank of England poised to raise rates but may push back on bets for more
full_text:
By Andy Bruce
MANCHESTER, England, Nov 2 (Reuters) - The Bank of England is expected to bow to inflation pressure from soaring energy costs and raise interest rates on Thursday, though it may push back against investors’ bets that several more increases will follow next year.
Economists polled by Reuters expect the BoE to raise Bank Rate to 4.0% from 3.75%, its first hike since August 2023, when inflation was still more than triple its 2% target.
The BoE was criticised for underestimating how persistent inflation would prove the last time energy costs surged, and it is wary of being caught out again, with global energy prices high and little sign of a lasting end to the Iran war.
Back then, the BoE was among the first major central banks to raise rates. This time the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank have moved first.
BANK OF ENGLAND’S HAND "INCREASINGLY FORCED"
Governor Andrew Bailey has said the BoE cannot wait for conclusive proof of second-round effects, where higher inflation feeds into wage- and price-setting, or it will act too late.
But how much evidence is enough, and whether the drawn-out Iran war makes some second-round effects inevitable, have divided the Monetary Policy Committee, which voted 6-3 to hold rates in September.
Bailey said last month that businesses he had spoken to seemed to be absorbing higher costs more than in 2022.
In September the BoE warned that inflation would rise above 4% early next year, and said the jump in energy prices since its July forecasts bore similarities to its "adverse" scenario, in which inflation risked becoming entrenched.
Inflation has since run hotter than the BoE expected. Consumer prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, compared with the central bank’s July forecast of 3.0%.
"In other words, their hands are increasingly being forced, whether they like it or not," said Stefan Koopman, senior macro strategist at Rabobank.
"At some point, even a committee that would probably rather sit tight has to make good on at least some of what is priced (in the market). That time is now."
SOME MPC MEMBERS HAVE CRITICISED THE BOE
The Reuters poll pointed to a 7-2 vote in favour of a hike, with external members Alan Taylor and Swati Dhingra seen as most likely to continue to vote to keep rates steady.
Both have stressed spare capacity in the economy as a reason to wait, though recent growth figures have surprised to the upside.
Hawkish policymakers such as Chief Economist Huw Pill and external members Catherine Mann and Megan Greene have criticised the BoE’s handling of the current episode.
But even they may baulk at endorsing market pricing of three to four more quarter-point hikes in 2027, which would take Bank Rate to between 4.75% and 5.0%.
"While we don’t expect a clear steer from the Committee on how many hikes they’re planning, it’s possible that the meeting minutes or Bailey ... signal that Bank Rate is unlikely to reach the level that is priced in by financial markets," said Alexander Harvey, UK economist at consultancy Oxford Economics.
STATEMENTS WILL OFFER CLUES TO RATES OUTLOOK
Harvey said individual MPC members’ statements would offer important clues to the outlook, particularly those of the BoE’s internal members, whose views have been finely balanced.
Unlike financial markets, economists polled by Reuters last month were split on whether further hikes would follow after November’s.
Mann has argued that aggressive bets on rate hikes reflect a risk premium the BoE itself exacerbated by adopting a "wait-and-see" stance after war broke out in the Middle East, rather than signalling clearly that it would keep inflation in check.
Alongside new economic forecasts, investors will be watching for the BoE’s initial assessment of finance minister John Healey’s budget, delivered last week.
Healey offered modest support to households and motorists struggling with higher energy costs, funded partly by a tax on banks. Economists said the measures would only slightly reduce the expected rise in inflation.

title: Oil slips more than 1% as talks continue on ending Iran war
full_text:
By Florence Tan
SINGAPORE, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Oil prices slipped more than 1% on Monday after Iranian and Qatari officials held a third straight day of talks aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Brent crude futures fell $1.59, or 1.40%, to $111.84 a barrel by 0011 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $102.56 a barrel, down $1.56, or 1.50%.
Brent ended October at its highest level in six months amid concerns that the US-Iran conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s US midterm elections.
"Oil is seeing a technical pullback this morning after last week’s strong gains," said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.
"Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now."
However, the market remained alert to the possibility that rhetoric around Iran could be ratcheted higher and push Brent toward $120 after the midterm elections, Waterer said.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that the purpose of the "ongoing and progressing" talks was to continue consultations with the Qatari mediators, adding Tehran is prepared for "both defence and diplomacy".
The talks come amid attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz that are driving up global energy and shipping costs. In October, Saudi Arabia increased crude exports versus September despite attacks by the Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis on its energy infrastructure, two of three ship-tracking companies said.
The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia, or OPEC+, kept December production targets steady on Sunday, confirming expectations that more policy adjustments will not occur until next year, as the group continues to struggle with export disruptions from the Iran war.
